scores.evidence: short-lived credentials for CI (for example, OIDC to your cloud) instead of stored keys
scores.rationale: All technical claims (OIDC federation, immutable SHA-tagged artifacts, GitOps version-bump PRs, admission-time policy enforcement) are accurate; the plan stays tool-agnostic so it never states deep guarantees, but nothing it depends on is wrong.

scores.evidence: Get a few services working end to end first, turn what you learn into reusable templates, and only then move the rest.
scores.rationale: It answers the sequencing question directly and is credibly buildable with a stated team, but implied core needs like database migration compatibility and flaky-test handling are absent.

scores.evidence: move services that others depend on (upstream) before the services that call them. That way contract tests have real providers
scores.rationale: Phases, data flows and decisions are mutually consistent with tight reasoning (pilot before templates, immutability honored everywhere, identity centralized in foundations) and no contradictions.

scores.evidence: Make rollback a single action and test it on purpose.
scores.rationale: Each phase has checkable 'Done when' gates, the riskiest assumptions (shared templates, rollback) are validated on a pilot before mass migration, and DORA dashboards against a Phase 0 baseline continue validation after launch.

scores.evidence: about 6–8 months to full migration. This varies a lot with how varied your services are
scores.rationale: Team size, timeline and service-type counts are clearly marked as rough estimates with sensitivity noted, though assumptions about compliance, budget and existing stack remain implicit.

scores.evidence: A template bug breaks many services | Versioned templates, testing of template changes, staged rollout
scores.rationale: Template blast radius, contract breakage and migration stall are handled concretely, but major domain failures—schema-migration/rollback incompatibility and an outage of the CI/CD platform itself—are missing.

scores.evidence: Platform observability: logs, metrics and alerts for the pipelines themselves.
scores.rationale: Deployment, rollback, pipeline monitoring, docs, support channel and a plausible 3–5 engineer platform team are covered, though incident response for the platform's own outages is not spelled out.

scores.evidence: Cost tuning for runners, caches and environments.
scores.rationale: People cost (team × duration) is estimated and runner/environment costs are named with controls like autoscaling, but there is no hosted-vs-self-hosted trade-off or compute cost estimate from build volume.

scores.evidence: Make the decisions that are hard to undo, and write each one down with its reasoning
scores.rationale: Hard-to-reverse choices are explicitly identified, documented with reasoning, and de-risked via pilot and versioned templates before mass migration, though explicit exit paths from the chosen vendors are not given.

scores.evidence: Keep per-service config to roughly 20 lines
scores.rationale: Every element earns its place—templates per type instead of 50 pipelines, report-only scans first, previews only where affordable—with a clear growth path in Phase 6 and no speculative machinery.

scores.evidence: Done when: the pilot services build green on every PR and main-branch builds produce signed, scanned, immutable artifacts.
scores.rationale: Build order is justified by dependencies, each phase has concrete first steps and checkable exit criteria, and adaptation paths exist (wave retrospectives, Wave 4 per-service decisions, report-only to blocking).

checklist.evidence: Group the services into types... Each type will get its own template.
Run old and new pipelines side by side for critical services until 2–3 production deploys on the new one have succeeded.
The same artifact moves forward through every environment and is never rebuilt.
short-lived credentials for CI (for example, OIDC to your cloud) instead of stored keys
critical vulnerabilities, unsigned images, missing SBOMs. Enforce this with policy-as-code (OPA/Kyverno) at the cluster's admission step.
Make rollback a single action and test it on purpose.
Add integration and contract tests to staging, because with 50 services, breaking another service's API is the main risk.
Ephemeral preview environments for each PR, where it's affordable.
aim for under 10 minutes for a PR build. Use caching, run steps in parallel, and only rebuild what changed.
Build runners/agents, autoscaling, with caching for dependencies and Docker layers.
Platform observability: logs, metrics and alerts for the pipelines themselves.
Deploy to production with an approval step at first, then gradually reduce manual steps.

traps.evidence: Don't migrate all 50 services until the shared pipeline has been proven on a small, varied pilot group.
tagged (immutable and tied to the commit SHA)
short-lived credentials for CI (for example, OIDC to your cloud) instead of stored keys
a pilot service goes from commit to production with no manual steps apart from an approval
CI engine (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, Buildkite, etc.)

note: A well-sequenced, trap-free migration plan with strong validation gates and proportionate design; its main gaps are database schema migration safety, flaky tests, fork-PR secret isolation, platform-outage planning, and compute cost estimation.
